### Previous Young Investigator Award Winners
##### 2025 Winner
**2025 Winner: Carolina Makowski, University of California, San Diego, USA**
Dr. Carolina Makowski is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of California San Diego (UCSD). She earned her BSc in Psychology and PhD in Neuroscience from McGill University, and completed her postdoctoral training in UCSD’s Department of Radiology. Her research bridges multiple scales of neuroscience to better understand the development of adolescent psychiatric disorders. She has a vested interest in identifying neurobiologically-informed predictive markers of eating disorders (e.g., through integration of multimodal MRI, genetics, and temperament) to meaningfully improve treatments for patients. Dr. Makowski’s research has been supported by the National Institutes of Mental Health, Brain Behavior Foundation, Kavli Institute for Brain and Mind, and by Canadian federal (Canadian Institutes of Health Research) and provincial (Fonds de Recherche du Quebec- Santé) funding mechanisms. Dr. Makowski is also an investigator within the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study Consortium, where she co-chairs the Professional Development Workgroup and is a member of the Image Analysis Workgroup. She has served in leadership and mentorship roles across multiple organizations, including the Organization for Human Brain Mapping, Flux Society, and UCSD’s Postdoctoral Teaching Group.

She is also a licensed Speech Language Pathologist specializing in pediatric language, literacy, and learning differences. The selection process for the Flux Awards is rigorous and thorough, ensuring that the most deserving candidates are chosen. This year, the Flux Awards Committee leadership selected members for subcommittees to ensure a broad range of experience, diversity, and inclusiveness across the Society.

After their individual reviews, the subcommittee members meet to discuss their evaluations and vote on a final candidate. The subcommittee then sends the nomination to the Flux Board of Directors, who review it to ensure fairness and avoid conflicts of interest. This process ensures that the most outstanding nominations from our esteemed community are recognized.

## **Laurel Joy Gabard-Durnam, Ph.D.**
_Northeastern University (Dept of Psychology and Institute for Cognitive and Brain Health)_

CNS 2027 | Young Investigator Award Lecture 1 - Mechanisms and Applications of Infant Sensory Neuroplasticity, Laurel Joy Gabard-Durnam, Ph.D.
Salons A-F The Young Investigator Award Lecture titled ''Mechanisms and Applications of Infant Sensory Neuroplasticity' will be held in person at the CNS 2027 Annual Meeting in Boston at the **Boston Marriott Copley Place Hotel** located at 110 Huntington Ave, Boston, MA 02116
Development is a period of remarkable plasticity when experiences can sculpt our brains and behavior in ways that last a lifetime. This biological embedding of experience confers both opportunity and vulnerability for learning and adaptation. However, much remains unanswered about _1) how brain mechanisms govern plasticity in human development, and 2) how experiences shape the plastic brain to scaffold emerging cognition and behavior._ I will share research pointing to a species-conserved role for GABA-ergic inhibition in developmentally modulating sensory cortex plasticity and share evidence for how these developmental shifts in inhibitory function support learning from external environmental cues to shape behavior. I will then share how a learner (infant) centric framework for parsing early life experiences can reveal not just what but how infants detect learnable information during these developmental windows of dynamic sensory plasticity. Finally, my team makes sustained efforts to expand which environments our field characterizes and who contributes to cognitive neuroscience research globally. I will share our ongoing efforts to combine original methods, open-source EEG software, and low-cost EEG hardware as a toolkit to detect individual infant neuroplasticity trajectories with fidelity in largescale cohort and randomized control trial projects in Sub-Saharan African contexts. In these ways, my research program aims to both better understand and support infant experience-dependent brain and cognitive development.

## From Time-Varying Neural Dynamics to Stable Cognitive Representations


## **Randolph Helfrich, M.D. , Ph.D**
_Yale University_
Monday, March 22, 2027, 2:00 pm - 2:30 pm, Salons A-F

CNS 2027 | Young Investigator Award Lecture 2 - From Time-Varying Neural Dynamics to Stable Cognitive Representations, Randolph Helfrich, M.D. , Ph.D.
Salons A-F The Young Investigator Award Lecture titled ''From Time-Varying Neural Dynamics to Stable Cognitive Representations will be held in person at the CNS 2027 Annual Meeting in Boston at the **Boston Marriott Copley Place Hotel** located at 110 Huntington Ave, Boston, MA 02116
The functional brain architecture underlying human cognition is ever-changing, as exemplified by the constantly waxing and waning neural activity patterns in the human electroencephalogram. Despite this time-varying nature of brain activity, we perceive the world as continuous, our movements unfold seamlessly, and we are able to form stable, long-lasting memories. This raises the question: how can ever-changing neural activity give rise to our continuous and coherent experience of the world? In this talk, I will outline an integrative cognitive neuroscience approach that bridges the gap between different species, scales, and modalities, focusing on intracranial human neurophysiology. I will first show that variable, seemingly noisy brain states reflect circuit-level excitability that systematically structures human behavior on a millisecond timescale. Building on this, I will demonstrate that such variability is not noise but an organizing principle. In human prefrontal cortex, increased neural variability during working memory expands the dimensionality of population activity, creating a representational geometry that supports the stable, flexible maintenance of information and its efficient readout by downstream motor systems. In sum, this talk aims to outline how intracranial human neurophysiology offers new insight into the neural computations that enable higher cognitive and mental functions. By linking macroscale neural correlates of behavior to microscale circuit properties and the geometry of population codes, this approach offers a step toward understanding the complex interplay between brain dynamics and cognitive functions.

## About the YIA Award
The purpose of the Young Investigator Award is to recognize outstanding contributions by scientists early in their career. Two awardees are named by the Awards Committee, and are honored at the CNS Annual meeting.

CNS 2027 | Young Investigator Award Lecture 1 - Mechanisms and Applications of Infant Sensory Neuroplasticity, Laurel Joy Gabard-Durnam, Ph.D.
Salons A-F The Young Investigator Award Lecture titled ''Mechanisms and Applications of Infant Sensory Neuroplasticity' will be held in person at the CNS 2027 Annual Meeting in Boston at the **Boston Marriott Copley Place Hotel** located at 110 Huntington Ave, Boston, MA 02116
Development is a period of remarkable plasticity when experiences can sculpt our brains and behavior in ways that last a lifetime. This biological embedding of experience confers both opportunity and vulnerability for learning and adaptation. However, much remains unanswered about _1) how brain mechanisms govern plasticity in human development, and 2) how experiences shape the plastic brain to scaffold emerging cognition and behavior._ I will share research pointing to a species-conserved role for GABA-ergic inhibition in developmentally modulating sensory cortex plasticity and share evidence for how these developmental shifts in inhibitory function support learning from external environmental cues to shape behavior. I will then share how a learner (infant) centric framework for parsing early life experiences can reveal not just what but how infants detect learnable information during these developmental windows of dynamic sensory plasticity. Finally, my team makes sustained efforts to expand which environments our field characterizes and who contributes to cognitive neuroscience research globally. I will share our ongoing efforts to combine original methods, open-source EEG software, and low-cost EEG hardware as a toolkit to detect individual infant neuroplasticity trajectories with fidelity in largescale cohort and randomized control trial projects in Sub-Saharan African contexts. In these ways, my research program aims to both better understand and support infant experience-dependent brain and cognitive development.

CNS 2027 | Young Investigator Award Lecture 2 - From Time-Varying Neural Dynamics to Stable Cognitive Representations, Randolph Helfrich, M.D. , Ph.D.
Salons A-F The Young Investigator Award Lecture titled ''From Time-Varying Neural Dynamics to Stable Cognitive Representations will be held in person at the CNS 2027 Annual Meeting in Boston at the **Boston Marriott Copley Place Hotel** located at 110 Huntington Ave, Boston, MA 02116
The functional brain architecture underlying human cognition is ever-changing, as exemplified by the constantly waxing and waning neural activity patterns in the human electroencephalogram. Despite this time-varying nature of brain activity, we perceive the world as continuous, our movements unfold seamlessly, and we are able to form stable, long-lasting memories. This raises the question: how can ever-changing neural activity give rise to our continuous and coherent experience of the world? In this talk, I will outline an integrative cognitive neuroscience approach that bridges the gap between different species, scales, and modalities, focusing on intracranial human neurophysiology. I will first show that variable, seemingly noisy brain states reflect circuit-level excitability that systematically structures human behavior on a millisecond timescale. Building on this, I will demonstrate that such variability is not noise but an organizing principle. In human prefrontal cortex, increased neural variability during working memory expands the dimensionality of population activity, creating a representational geometry that supports the stable, flexible maintenance of information and its efficient readout by downstream motor systems. In sum, this talk aims to outline how intracranial human neurophysiology offers new insight into the neural computations that enable higher cognitive and mental functions. By linking macroscale neural correlates of behavior to microscale circuit properties and the geometry of population codes, this approach offers a step toward understanding the complex interplay between brain dynamics and cognitive functions.

# Awards Selection Process
The selection process for the Flux Awards is rigorous and thorough, ensuring that the most deserving candidates are chosen. This year, the Flux Awards Committee leadership selected members for subcommittees to ensure a broad range of experience, diversity, and inclusiveness across the Society.
These subcommittee members carefully review and evaluate the nominations based on the nominees’ contributions to the field, the impact of their research, and their commitment to advancing our understanding of developmental cognitive neuroscience. They pay careful attention to avoid conflicts of interest throughout the process.
After their individual reviews, the subcommittee members meet to discuss their evaluations and vote on a final candidate. The subcommittee then sends the nomination to the Flux Board of Directors, who review it to ensure fairness and avoid conflicts of interest. This process ensures that the most outstanding nominations from our esteemed community are recognized.

Salons A-F The Young Investigator Award Lecture titled ''Mechanisms and Applications of Infant Sensory Neuroplasticity' will be held in person at the CNS 2027 Annual Meeting in Boston at the **Boston Marriott Copley Place Hotel** located at 110 Huntington Ave, Boston, MA 02116
Development is a period of remarkable plasticity when experiences can sculpt our brains and behavior in ways that last a lifetime. This biological embedding of experience confers both opportunity and vulnerability for learning and adaptation. However, much remains unanswered about _1) how brain mechanisms govern plasticity in human development, and 2) how experiences shape the plastic brain to scaffold emerging cognition and behavior._ I will share research pointing to a species-conserved role for GABA-ergic inhibition in developmentally modulating sensory cortex plasticity and share evidence for how these developmental shifts in inhibitory function support learning from external environmental cues to shape behavior. I will then share how a learner (infant) centric framework for parsing early life experiences can reveal not just what but how infants detect learnable information during these developmental windows of dynamic sensory plasticity. Finally, my team makes sustained efforts to expand which environments our field characterizes and who contributes to cognitive neuroscience research globally. I will share our ongoing efforts to combine original methods, open-source EEG software, and low-cost EEG hardware as a toolkit to detect individual infant neuroplasticity trajectories with fidelity in largescale cohort and randomized control trial projects in Sub-Saharan African contexts. In these ways, my research program aims to both better understand and support infant experience-dependent brain and cognitive development.

Salons A-F The Young Investigator Award Lecture titled ''From Time-Varying Neural Dynamics to Stable Cognitive Representations will be held in person at the CNS 2027 Annual Meeting in Boston at the **Boston Marriott Copley Place Hotel** located at 110 Huntington Ave, Boston, MA 02116
The functional brain architecture underlying human cognition is ever-changing, as exemplified by the constantly waxing and waning neural activity patterns in the human electroencephalogram. Despite this time-varying nature of brain activity, we perceive the world as continuous, our movements unfold seamlessly, and we are able to form stable, long-lasting memories. This raises the question: how can ever-changing neural activity give rise to our continuous and coherent experience of the world? In this talk, I will outline an integrative cognitive neuroscience approach that bridges the gap between different species, scales, and modalities, focusing on intracranial human neurophysiology. I will first show that variable, seemingly noisy brain states reflect circuit-level excitability that systematically structures human behavior on a millisecond timescale. Building on this, I will demonstrate that such variability is not noise but an organizing principle. In human prefrontal cortex, increased neural variability during working memory expands the dimensionality of population activity, creating a representational geometry that supports the stable, flexible maintenance of information and its efficient readout by downstream motor systems. In sum, this talk aims to outline how intracranial human neurophysiology offers new insight into the neural computations that enable higher cognitive and mental functions. By linking macroscale neural correlates of behavior to microscale circuit properties and the geometry of population codes, this approach offers a step toward understanding the complex interplay between brain dynamics and cognitive functions.
